summary: This workshop-style Photoshop workflow demonstrates landscape focus stacking to preserve sharp foreground and background detail, using multiple exposures loaded into a stack, auto-alignment, and content-aware blending. After revealing the focus-stacking process, the instructor discusses cropping decisions (including a four-by-five aspect) and explains focus-breathing-related border artifacts. The tutorial then proceeds to color-grade the image, emphasizing sunset tones through targeted adjustments (color balance, camera calibration, and selective midtone control) and painting light onto the mountains. It culminates with Dodge/Burn and glow techniques, sponge-tool enhancements, hard vignette, and depth cues to push distant mountains further away, with explicit scene identification of McKinnon Peak and McKinnon Hut as reference points within the shot.

sections.title: Focus stacking setup and alignment in Photoshop
sections.description: The instructor introduces the broader concept of focus stacking when using a wider lens, then demonstrates loading a background and a foreground into a Photoshop stack, auto-aligning the layers, and blending with content-aware fill. The dialogue notes that Helicon Focus is a strong stand-alone option but Photoshop can perform focus stacking as well, with results that are rarely perfect but usable. The section also mentions the difference between stacking versus using a dedicated tool and frames the workflow around later color adjustment.

sections.title: Cropping decisions and focus breathing considerations
sections.description: After blending, the content is flattened and cropped to the preferred aspect ratio (4x5). The presenter explains that borders can appear due to focus breathing—as the lens changes focus, the image framing shifts slightly—and demonstrates cropping to manage these effects while preserving the intended composition.

sections.title: Color grading and sky-mountain separation
sections.description: This section covers adjusting the overall color tone to emphasize sunset colors while isolating sky and mountain areas. The workflow includes reducing shadows, tweaking whites/ exposure, then leveraging color balance and calibration to push sky pinks/blues and the mountain tones into a complementary palette that preserves mood without over-saturating grass and foreground elements.

sections.title: Local adjustments, glow, and depth control
concepts: Dodge vs Burn tool and color impact

Enhancing depth via distant mountain colorization
sections.description: The instructor delves into localized post-processing: using dodge and burn to influence light and color across midtones, highlights, and shadows; applying a glow with the sponge tool; painting light on the mountain to simulate directional light from the right; introducing a hard vignette to steer the viewer toward the main subject; subtly desaturating/adjusting distant mountains with blue/purple tones to create depth. The segment also demonstrates iterative editing (painting, erasing, re-checking) to maintain natural edges and depth cues, and includes remarks about the dodge tool’s color behavior and its long-standing role in their workflow.
